result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.cycle_basis()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find a fundamental cycle basis of the graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L21717-L21804){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.cycle_basis(root=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Cycle basis](/assets/graphs/cycle-basis.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The house-shaped graph has 6 edges and 5 nodes, so a cycle basis has 6 − 5 + 1 = 2 cycles. Building the BFS tree from root A (node id 1) gives the fundamental cycles B, A, C (accent color) and D, B, A, C, E (teal), each closed by one non-tree edge." width="100%"} A cycle basis is a minimal set of cycles such that any cycle in the graph can be expressed as a symmetric difference (XOR) of cycles in the basis. For a connected graph with `V` vertices and `E` edges, the cycle basis has exactly `E - V + 1` cycles (the cyclomatic complexity). The algorithm builds a spanning tree using BFS from a root node, then for each non-tree edge (back edge), finds the fundamental cycle it creates with the tree. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [root]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional root node ID to start BFS from. If `None`, uses an arbitrary node. Different root nodes may produce different (but equally valid) cycle bases. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[list[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A list of cycles forming the cycle basis. Each cycle is a list of node IDs. The cycles are fundamental cycles (each contains exactly one back edge). ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If called on a directed graph (cycle basis only applies to undirected graphs). [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the specified root node does not exist in the graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The cyclomatic number $E - V + C$ (with $C$ the number of connected components) fixes the size of *every* fundamental cycle basis, so what varies between choices is only which cycles appear, not how many. Building one takes $O(V + E)$: a BFS spanning tree covers the tree edges, and each of the remaining $E - V + C$ back edges closes a unique fundamental cycle. Different `root=` choices, or different spanning trees more generally, produce different but equally valid bases. Disconnected graphs are handled component by component. If total edge weight matters, `minimum_cycle_basis()` finds the basis of least weight. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A square with one diagonal splits into two triangular fundamental cycles: ::: {#3e502dfe .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec # Square with diagonal graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges( [ ("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "A"), ("A", "C"), # diagonal ] ) ) basis = graph.cycle_basis() len(basis) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: Passing a specific `root=` changes which spanning tree is built, but the number of fundamental cycles stays the same -- always `E - V + 1` for a connected graph: ::: {#ff7fbcde .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A")]) ) node_ids = graph.get_node_ids() basis = graph.cycle_basis(root=node_ids[0]) len(basis) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 1 ``` ::: :::
